intro: In 1999, a housing developer saw a marble sculpture of a twisting torso and asked the sculptor: could you build that as a tower? Six years later, Malmo had a 190-meter residential skyscraper that rotates 90 degrees from base to top.
page_title: Turning Torso: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The Turning Torso began as a white marble sculpture by Santiago Calatrava, a study of a human body twisting as far as it can while staying upright. In 1999 Johnny Orback, managing director of the Malmo branch of the cooperative housing association HSB, saw the sculpture in a brochure for Calatrava's entry in the Oresund Bridge architectural competition. He travelled to Zurich and asked Calatrava to design a residential building on the same idea: a stack of cubes rotating around a core. Construction started on 14 February 2001 in Malmo's Western Harbor, a former shipyard area being remade as a sustainable waterfront district. The tower was completed on 27 August 2005 and opened on 1 November 2005.
sections.heading: From sculpture to skyscraper

sections.body: The tower is nine box units, each five floors high, stacked around a concrete core and each twisted a little further than the one below. The top cube sits 90 degrees clockwise from the ground floor, about 1.6 degrees of rotation per floor. The core is a concrete pipe 10.6 meters across inside, with walls 2.5 meters thick at the ground floor tapering to 0.4 meters at the top, carrying the lifts and stairs. Each floor is an irregular pentagon: a square section around the core plus a triangular part carried by the external steel structure. A white steel exoskeleton climbs the front face, a tapered spine column at the corner of each floor with horizontal and diagonal tubes reaching back to anchors at the rear, damping the tower's vibration in the wind off the Oresund strait. The facade is curved aluminum panels with windows leaning in or out to follow the twist. At 190 meters with 54 floors and 147 apartments, it was the tallest building in the Nordic region until Karlatornet in Gothenburg passed it in September 2022.
sections.heading: How the twist stands up

sections.body: Malmo built the Torso partly to give itself a new skyline. The city's symbol had been the Kockums Crane, a giant shipyard crane less than a kilometer away that was dismantled in 2002, and local politicians wanted the residents to have a new landmark for the post-industrial city. The two bottom cubes hold offices; cubes three through nine hold the apartments. Floors 49 to 54 are public and semi-public: an observation deck, a club, a restaurant, and conference floors with 360-degree views over Malmo and Copenhagen across the strait. The project won the 2005 Gold Emporis Skyscraper Award and the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat's 10 Year Award in 2015. It also ran to more than twice its budgeted cost, and the apartments, first meant to be sold, ended up being let when buyers stayed away.
sections.heading: A new symbol for Malmo

sections.body:
The Discovery Channel filmed the tower while it was still rising: an episode of Extreme Engineering showed how a floor of the twisting building was constructed, and the program aired first in the United States in the fall of 2004. A Swedish documentary, The Socialist, the Architect and the Twisted Tower (2005), told the behind-the-scenes story of Orback risking his reputation and Calatrava designing his first skyscraper, a film about a social-democratic housing association commissioning a world-famous architect.

The tower's most famous single moment involved no camera crew at all. On 18 August 2006 the Austrian skydiver Felix Baumgartner, years before his Stratos jump, parachuted onto the Turning Torso and then jumped off it, using the brand-new landmark as a launch pad. The stunt cemented the building's image as Malmo's daredevil symbol: a residential tower famous enough to jump off.

timeline.text: HSB Malmo's Johnny Orback sees Calatrava's Twisting Torso sculpture and commissions a residential tower on the same idea.
Construction starts in Malmo's Western Harbor.
The Kockums Crane, the shipyard crane the tower is meant to replace as Malmo's symbol, is dismantled.
Discovery Channel's Extreme Engineering films the tower's construction.
The tower is completed at 190 meters; it wins the Gold Emporis Skyscraper Award.
Felix Baumgartner parachutes onto the tower and jumps off it.
The tower receives the CTBUH 10 Year Award.
Karlatornet in Gothenburg surpasses it as the Nordic region's tallest building.
